screens.title: What is a deployment script?
screens.narratorSegment: A deployment script is a JavaScript file in your Hardhat project that automates deploying a compiled smart contract to a blockchain. At its core the script uses ethers. js, which Hardhat exposes, to obtain a ContractFactory for the compiled contract. The ContractFactory knows the compiled bytecode and ABI and provides a deploy method that sends a deployment transaction. In practice you write an async main function that calls ethers. getContractFactory with your contract name, then calls factory. deploy with any constructor arguments, and then awaits factoryInstance. deployed() to ensure the deployment transaction is mined. A concrete example from this chapter is obtaining MyToken via ethers. getContractFactory('MyToken'), then calling MyToken. deploy('My Awesome Token', 'MAT') when the constructor accepts name and symbol. A common misconception is that deploy() alone completes deployment; in reality deploy() initiates the transaction and you must await deployed() to get a confirmed contract address. Key benefits of using a script are repeatability, clear terminal output for addresses and transaction hashes, and the ability to run against different networks simply by changing the --network flag. Try thinking of the script as a repeatable recipe that records the final address you will use to interact with the contract.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A deployment script automates the steps to publish a contract using a ContractFactory, deploy(), and deployed() calls.

content.html:
Core Concept
Deployment Script
A repeatable JavaScript file that uses ethers.js to deploy a compiled contract and report the address and transaction hash.
Why it matters
It lets you automate trusted deployments and reproduce the same steps across environments.
Misconception
Calling deploy() alone does not guarantee the contract is confirmed; you must await deployed() to ensure mining.
Example
// pseudo-pattern used in many scripts
const { ethers } = require('hardhat');

async function main() {
  const MyToken = await ethers.getContractFactory('MyToken');
  const token = await MyToken.deploy('My Awesome Token', 'MAT');
  await token.deployed();
  console.log(`Deployed to: ${'${token.address}'}`);
}

main().catch((e) => console.error(e));
Anatomy of a script
  • Import ethers from Hardhat to access ContractFactory functions.
  • Get a ContractFactory for the compiled contract name.
  • Call deploy with constructor arguments if required and await deployed() for confirmation.
  • Log myContract.address and myContract.deployTransaction.hash for later use.
Key Takeaway

Treat deployment scripts as repeatable recipes: they should record addresses and wait for confirmations to avoid race conditions.

screens.title: Using ethers.getContractFactory
screens.narratorSegment: The ContractFactory is the ethers. js abstraction that knows how to deploy a particular compiled contract. When you call ethers. getContractFactory with the contract name, Hardhat returns an object wired to the contract's ABI and bytecode as produced by the build step. This ContractFactory exposes a deploy method that packages constructor arguments and creates a deployment transaction. For example, a typical line is const Counter = await ethers. getContractFactory('Counter'); which provides you with the factory object. A common misconception is to treat the factory as an instance of the contract; it is not. The factory creates instances. Once you call const counter = await Counter. deploy(), counter is the Contract object representing the deployed instance, while Counter remains able to deploy more instances. Practically, using the factory pattern clarifies roles: compilation yields bytecode, the factory sends the deployment transaction, and the returned Contract includes the address and the deployTransaction. hash. When debugging, confirm the contract name matches the compiled artifact name and that compilation has run successfully; a mismatch is a frequent source of errors. Finally, remember that factories are synchronous to obtain but asynchronous when deploying because blockchain confirmation requires awaiting deployed().

keyIdea.title: ContractFactory role
keyIdea.text: A ContractFactory is a deployer for a specific compiled contract and must be used to create Contract instances via deploy().

content.html:
Process
Get ContractFactory
The factory contains compiled bytecode and the ABI and provides the deploy method to create a contract instance.
Code pattern
const { ethers } = require('hardhat');

async function main() {
  const Counter = await ethers.getContractFactory('Counter');
  // Counter is a factory, not an instance
  const counter = await Counter.deploy();
  await counter.deployed();
  console.log('Counter deployed to:', counter.address);
}

main().catch((e) => console.error(e));
Key points
  • Factory binds ABI and bytecode for deployment.
  • Call factory.deploy(...args) to start deployment.
  • Factory can deploy multiple instances; the returned Contract is a specific instance.
  • Verify the contract name matches the compiled artifact to avoid runtime errors.
Pro tip
If getContractFactory throws, run a fresh compile and confirm the artifact name exactly matches the contract name used.
Key Takeaway

ContractFactory is the deploy-time blueprint; preserve the distinction between factory and instance to avoid confusion.

screens.title: deploy() and deployed() — asynchronous deployment
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between deploy() and deployed() is critical for reliable deployments. Calling factory. deploy(...) constructs and broadcasts the transaction that will create the contract on-chain, and it returns a Contract object immediately that contains the deployTransaction details. However, that Contract is not yet guaranteed to exist on the blockchain until the transaction is mined. The deployed() method is an asynchronous wait that resolves once the deployment transaction is confirmed. If you omit await contract. deployed(), subsequent code that assumes the contract exists — for instance attempting to call a function or reading the address — can fail because the node may not yet reflect the new contract. A practical pattern is to log the deployTransaction. hash right after deploy to capture the transaction identifier, then await deployed() and log contract. address when the contract is available. A common mistake is relying on rapid local confirmation semantics and forgetting that public testnets can take longer; always await deployed() before interacting with the contract and build retry or error handling around network delays. This distinction prevents race conditions between initiation and confirmation.

keyIdea.title: Asynchronous confirmation
keyIdea.text: deploy() starts the transaction and returns a Contract with deployTransaction; await deployed() ensures the contract exists on-chain.

content.html:
Process Flow
Initiate → Confirm
deploy() initiates the on-chain creation; deployed() waits for the mining confirmation that makes the contract address usable.
// pattern to capture both identifiers
const token = await MyToken.deploy('Name','SYM');
console.log('deploy tx hash:', token.deployTransaction.hash);
await token.deployed();
console.log('contract address:', token.address);
Explanation and common pitfalls
  • deploy() returns a Contract object immediately, but the blockchain state may not include it until mined.
  • deployed() resolves when the deployment transaction is mined and the address is valid for interaction.
  • On public testnets confirmation times vary; always await deployed() before calling contract methods.
Common mistake
Skipping await deployed() leads to failed interactions because the contract may not yet exist at the address you expect.
Key Takeaway

Always await the confirmation step to guarantee the blockchain has recorded the new contract before proceeding.

screens.title: Passing constructor arguments
screens.narratorSegment: When your contract defines a constructor that requires arguments, you pass those arguments directly into deploy(). The deployment call packages them into the transaction so the contract's initial state is set during creation. For example, a token contract with constructor(string name, string symbol) must be deployed with MyToken. deploy('My Awesome Token', 'MAT'). Forgetting to include required constructor arguments is a common error that causes the deploy call to fail immediately with a mismatch or missing parameter error. Another class of mistake is passing the wrong types, for example passing a number where a string is required or forgetting to format addresses and large numeric values correctly. In practice you should verify the contract constructor signature in your Solidity source or compiled artifact before forming the deploy call. A helpful pattern is to explicitly list arguments in the script and log them before calling deploy so you can confirm types at runtime. If you encounter a constructor mismatch, recompile and double-check the contract name and signature used with getContractFactory and deploy. This reduces guesswork during testnet deployments and avoids wasted gas on failed transactions.

keyIdea.title: Constructor args
keyIdea.text: Provide constructor parameters directly to deploy(), matching types and order exactly as declared in the contract.

content.html:
Definition
Pass constructor arguments
Constructor arguments are supplied to deploy() in the same order and types as the Solidity constructor declaration.
// Token example
const Token = await ethers.getContractFactory('MyToken');
const token = await Token.deploy('My Awesome Token', 'MAT');
await token.deployed();
console.log(token.address);
Common errors and checks
  • Missing arguments: deploy() fails because constructor signature is not satisfied.
  • Wrong types: pass strings for string parameters, addresses as strings, and use BigNumber or string for large integers.
  • Mismatched names: ensure getContractFactory uses the correct contract name matching the compiled artifact.
Quick check
Log your arguments before deploy to confirm they match the constructor and avoid sending transactions with incorrect initialization.
Key Takeaway

Match types and order exactly when passing constructor arguments to avoid immediate deployment failures.

screens.title: Executing deployment scripts with Hardhat CLI
screens.narratorSegment: Running deployment scripts is done through the Hardhat CLI using the npx hardhat run command. For a local node, you use npx hardhat run scripts/deploy_counter. js --network localhost to target the Hardhat Network or an HTTP endpoint you run locally. When targeting a public testnet like Sepolia, supply the configured network name, for example npx hardhat run scripts/deploy_counter. js --network sepolia. Before doing so ensure hardhat. config. js includes the RPC URL and the private key for the account that will pay for gas. A frequent pitfall is misconfiguring the RPC or using a mainnet private key in a test script. For local runs, confirmations are immediate which makes iteration fast; for testnets expect slower confirmation times and always await deployed() before continuing. The CLI prints terminal output including console. log statements from your script, so it’s common to log the deploy transaction hash and the contract address. Use these logs to verify success. If an error occurs, Hardhat’s stack trace typically points to the script line or even a contract trace; read it to locate configuration or code issues.

Process
Run with the Hardhat CLI
Execute scripts locally or on a named network using the --network flag and ensure configuration is correct beforehand.
// Local deployment
npx hardhat run scripts/deploy_counter.js --network localhost

// Testnet deployment

  • Verify hardhat.config.js has RPC URL and private key set for the target network.

screens.title: Interpreting deployment output
screens.narratorSegment: After a successful deployment you will typically see two crucial pieces of information printed by your script: the contract address and the deployment transaction hash. The contract address is the permanent on-chain identifier you use to interact with the deployed contract. The deployment transaction hash is the identifier for the transaction that created the contract; you can use it to look up the transaction on a block explorer or to confirm inclusion in a block. A common source of confusion is expecting the address to appear before confirmation — remember that the address may be known immediately after the transaction is created in some local nodes, but that address is only safe to use after await deployed() confirms mining. Another practical difference: the transaction hash is useful when diagnosing failed deployments because it links to the transaction receipt and any revert messages, while the address indicates success and will be used by front ends and scripts to connect to the contract. Practically, log both values and store them in your deployment records so future automation and verification tasks can reference them reliably.

Explanation
Address vs Transaction Hash
Both are important: the address is your contract's identifier; the transaction hash links to the creation event for auditing and troubleshooting.
Contract Address
A permanent identifier for interacting with your contract after confirmation.
Deployment Transaction Hash
An audit trail for the creation transaction; useful when diagnosing reverts or network issues.
Practical example
Deploying Counter contract...
Counter contract deployed to: 0xAbc123...def
Deployment transaction hash: 0x9f8a...456
Store both values in your deployment logs. The transaction hash helps you confirm block inclusion if the address does not appear immediately on external services.
Key Takeaway

Capture and preserve both contract addresses and transaction hashes as part of every deployment for traceability and subsequent interactions.

screens.title: Common deployment errors and fixes
screens.narratorSegment: When a deployment fails, the terminal is your primary diagnostic tool. The most frequent causes listed in the chapter are insufficient funds, an incorrect private key, an invalid RPC URL, wrong constructor arguments, and forgetting to wait for deployed(). Insufficient funds result in a transaction rejection or out-of-gas errors; the fix is to top up the test account with faucet ETH or use a funded test wallet. An incorrect private key prevents signing; double-check the key in your configuration and use a dedicated test wallet. An invalid RPC URL prevents connecting to the network and usually causes immediate connection errors; confirm the URL and network name in hardhat. config. js. Constructor argument mismatches show up as runtime errors when deploy() rejects because the ABI and provided args differ. Finally, forgetting await deployed() causes later interactions to fail; ensure you await confirmation before calling contract methods. Hardhat provides stack traces pointing to the failing script line; read them carefully. A good troubleshooting workflow is: read the error, check balance and key, verify RPC, and re-run with logging to isolate the issue.

keyIdea.text: Check account balance, private key, RPC URL, constructor args, and ensure you awaited deployed() when diagnosing deployment failures.

content.html:
Comparison
Error → Likely cause → Fix
Insufficient funds
Top up the deploying account with test ETH from a faucet or use another funded wallet.
Incorrect private key
Confirm the private key in hardhat.config.js and ensure it's the test wallet, not your main wallet.
Invalid RPC URL
Verify the RPC endpoint and network name; try connecting with a simple provider call to confirm reachability.
More errors
Constructor argument mismatch
Re-check the constructor signature and pass arguments in the correct order and type.
Missing await deployed()
Add await contract.deployed() to ensure mining before subsequent interactions.
Troubleshooting checklist
Read the stack trace, verify balance and key, confirm RPC reachability, recompile contracts, and re-run the script with logging.
Reflective question

If your script shows a transaction hash but interactions fail, which of the checklist steps will you check first and why?

screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks through deploying a simple Counter contract so you can practice writing and running a deploy script. Run the script locally with npx hardhat run scripts/deploy_counter. js --network localhost for quick feedback. If you later want to test on Sepolia, ensure the test wallet is funded and your hardhat. config. js includes the RPC URL and private key before running with --network sepolia. keyIdea.text: Follow the provided Counter contract and deploy script to practice compiling, deploying, awaiting confirmation, and recording outputs.

content.html:
Step-by-step
Counter contract and deploy script
Create the contract, write the script, compile, then run the CLI to deploy locally or to a testnet.
Counter.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

contract Counter {
  uint public count;

  constructor() {
    count = 0;
  }

  function increment() public {
    count++;
  }

  function decrement() public {
    count--;
  }
}
deploy_counter.js
const { ethers } = require('hardhat');

async function main() {
  const Counter = await ethers.getContractFactory('Counter');
  console.log('Deploying Counter contract...');
  const counter = await Counter.deploy();
  await counter.deployed();

  console.log(`Counter contract deployed to: ${'${counter.address}'}`);
  console.log(`Deployment transaction hash: ${'${counter.deployTransaction.hash}'}`);
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});
Run locally: npx hardhat run scripts/deploy_counter.js --network localhost. For Sepolia, ensure your wallet has test ETH and run with --network sepolia after configuring RPC and key.
Key Takeaway

This activity ties compilation, script writing, CLI execution, and output recording into a single deploy cycle you can repeat and adapt.

What to Remember
A final checklist for safe deployments.
Await deployed()
Ensure the blockchain has mined the deployment before interacting with the contract.
Match constructor args

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn the full practical workflow for taking a compiled Solidity contract from your project and placing it on a blockchain using Hardhat. You will see how deployment scripts are simple JavaScript files that use ethers. js to obtain a ContractFactory, call deploy with any constructor arguments, and wait for the transaction to be mined. We’ll practice with a small Counter contract and a token-style example that accepts a name and symbol. You will also learn how to run those scripts locally for fast iteration and how to run them on a public testnet when you need external verification. Along the way we’ll cover the deployment outputs you must record — the contract address and transaction hash — and common mistakes such as missing constructor arguments, incorrect RPC configuration, or forgetting to wait for the contract to be confirmed. By the end you’ll be able to write a reliable deploy script, run it with the Hardhat CLI, and interpret any terminal output to proceed safely.

These objectives guide your practice with Hardhat deployments. First, you will understand the essential steps: compile, prepare a ContractFactory, call deploy, and wait for confirmation. That mental model helps you reason about asynchronous blockchain operations. Second, you will learn to write a deployment script that uses ethers. js to obtain the ContractFactory and to pass constructor arguments when needed; this is the exact code pattern you will reuse across projects. Third, you will execute scripts both against a local Hardhat node for quick iteration and against a public testnet when you need external validation, so you can observe differences in confirmation times and required configuration. Fourth, you will interpret deployment output — specifically the contract address and the deployment transaction hash — and record them for later interaction or verification. Each objective emphasizes a practical skill: writing code, running commands, and reading results so you can deploy reliably.

This second objectives slide focuses on practicing and verifying the earlier skills. You will learn how to run the Hardhat CLI command with the --network flag to connect to either a localhost node or a named testnet; this practice shows the difference between fast local confirmations and slower public confirmations. You will also practice reading the two key outputs after deployment: the contract address you will use for future interaction and the transaction hash that links to the blockchain record. Another objective pairs execution with configuration: verifying that your hardhat. config. js contains the correct RPC URL and the deploying account private key so the script can broadcast transactions. Finally, you will practice troubleshooting common errors by reading Hardhat's stack traces and terminal messages, and by confirming that test wallets have sufficient test ETH. Each objective is actionable so you can verify your competency by running a real deploy and recording the expected outputs.

A deployment script is a JavaScript file in your Hardhat project that automates deploying a compiled smart contract to a blockchain. At its core the script uses ethers. js, which Hardhat exposes, to obtain a ContractFactory for the compiled contract. The ContractFactory knows the compiled bytecode and ABI and provides a deploy method that sends a deployment transaction. In practice you write an async main function that calls ethers. getContractFactory with your contract name, then calls factory. deploy with any constructor arguments, and then awaits factoryInstance. deployed() to ensure the deployment transaction is mined. A concrete example from this chapter is obtaining MyToken via ethers. getContractFactory('MyToken'), then calling MyToken. deploy('My Awesome Token', 'MAT') when the constructor accepts name and symbol. A common misconception is that deploy() alone completes deployment; in reality deploy() initiates the transaction and you must await deployed() to get a confirmed contract address. Key benefits of using a script are repeatability, clear terminal output for addresses and transaction hashes, and the ability to run against different networks simply by changing the --network flag. Try thinking of the script as a repeatable recipe that records the final address you will use to interact with the contract.

The ContractFactory is the ethers. js abstraction that knows how to deploy a particular compiled contract. When you call ethers. getContractFactory with the contract name, Hardhat returns an object wired to the contract's ABI and bytecode as produced by the build step. This ContractFactory exposes a deploy method that packages constructor arguments and creates a deployment transaction. For example, a typical line is const Counter = await ethers. getContractFactory('Counter'); which provides you with the factory object. A common misconception is to treat the factory as an instance of the contract; it is not. The factory creates instances. Once you call const counter = await Counter. deploy(), counter is the Contract object representing the deployed instance, while Counter remains able to deploy more instances. Practically, using the factory pattern clarifies roles: compilation yields bytecode, the factory sends the deployment transaction, and the returned Contract includes the address and the deployTransaction. hash. When debugging, confirm the contract name matches the compiled artifact name and that compilation has run successfully; a mismatch is a frequent source of errors. Finally, remember that factories are synchronous to obtain but asynchronous when deploying because blockchain confirmation requires awaiting deployed().

Understanding the difference between deploy() and deployed() is critical for reliable deployments. Calling factory. deploy(...) constructs and broadcasts the transaction that will create the contract on-chain, and it returns a Contract object immediately that contains the deployTransaction details. However, that Contract is not yet guaranteed to exist on the blockchain until the transaction is mined. The deployed() method is an asynchronous wait that resolves once the deployment transaction is confirmed. If you omit await contract. deployed(), subsequent code that assumes the contract exists — for instance attempting to call a function or reading the address — can fail because the node may not yet reflect the new contract. A practical pattern is to log the deployTransaction. hash right after deploy to capture the transaction identifier, then await deployed() and log contract. address when the contract is available. A common mistake is relying on rapid local confirmation semantics and forgetting that public testnets can take longer; always await deployed() before interacting with the contract and build retry or error handling around network delays. This distinction prevents race conditions between initiation and confirmation.

When your contract defines a constructor that requires arguments, you pass those arguments directly into deploy(). The deployment call packages them into the transaction so the contract's initial state is set during creation. For example, a token contract with constructor(string name, string symbol) must be deployed with MyToken. deploy('My Awesome Token', 'MAT'). Forgetting to include required constructor arguments is a common error that causes the deploy call to fail immediately with a mismatch or missing parameter error. Another class of mistake is passing the wrong types, for example passing a number where a string is required or forgetting to format addresses and large numeric values correctly. In practice you should verify the contract constructor signature in your Solidity source or compiled artifact before forming the deploy call. A helpful pattern is to explicitly list arguments in the script and log them before calling deploy so you can confirm types at runtime. If you encounter a constructor mismatch, recompile and double-check the contract name and signature used with getContractFactory and deploy. This reduces guesswork during testnet deployments and avoids wasted gas on failed transactions.

Running deployment scripts is done through the Hardhat CLI using the npx hardhat run command. For a local node, you use npx hardhat run scripts/deploy_counter. js --network localhost to target the Hardhat Network or an HTTP endpoint you run locally. When targeting a public testnet like Sepolia, supply the configured network name, for example npx hardhat run scripts/deploy_counter. js --network sepolia. Before doing so ensure hardhat. config. js includes the RPC URL and the private key for the account that will pay for gas. A frequent pitfall is misconfiguring the RPC or using a mainnet private key in a test script. For local runs, confirmations are immediate which makes iteration fast; for testnets expect slower confirmation times and always await deployed() before continuing. The CLI prints terminal output including console. log statements from your script, so it’s common to log the deploy transaction hash and the contract address. Use these logs to verify success. If an error occurs, Hardhat’s stack trace typically points to the script line or even a contract trace; read it to locate configuration or code issues.

After a successful deployment you will typically see two crucial pieces of information printed by your script: the contract address and the deployment transaction hash. The contract address is the permanent on-chain identifier you use to interact with the deployed contract. The deployment transaction hash is the identifier for the transaction that created the contract; you can use it to look up the transaction on a block explorer or to confirm inclusion in a block. A common source of confusion is expecting the address to appear before confirmation — remember that the address may be known immediately after the transaction is created in some local nodes, but that address is only safe to use after await deployed() confirms mining. Another practical difference: the transaction hash is useful when diagnosing failed deployments because it links to the transaction receipt and any revert messages, while the address indicates success and will be used by front ends and scripts to connect to the contract. Practically, log both values and store them in your deployment records so future automation and verification tasks can reference them reliably.

When a deployment fails, the terminal is your primary diagnostic tool. The most frequent causes listed in the chapter are insufficient funds, an incorrect private key, an invalid RPC URL, wrong constructor arguments, and forgetting to wait for deployed(). Insufficient funds result in a transaction rejection or out-of-gas errors; the fix is to top up the test account with faucet ETH or use a funded test wallet. An incorrect private key prevents signing; double-check the key in your configuration and use a dedicated test wallet. An invalid RPC URL prevents connecting to the network and usually causes immediate connection errors; confirm the URL and network name in hardhat. config. js. Constructor argument mismatches show up as runtime errors when deploy() rejects because the ABI and provided args differ. Finally, forgetting await deployed() causes later interactions to fail; ensure you await confirmation before calling contract methods. Hardhat provides stack traces pointing to the failing script line; read them carefully. A good troubleshooting workflow is: read the error, check balance and key, verify RPC, and re-run with logging to isolate the issue.
